questions.q: What is the programme mainly about?
options: How to be happy by living in Denmark
How culture shapes the way we show sadness
Why so many young children feel sad
The history of the British Empire
questions.why: Neil says they'll investigate how the way people express sadness is influenced by their culture.

questions.q: What decision did Helen Russell make as a small child?
options: To become a writer
To move abroad
To be happy
To study emotions
questions.why: After her baby sister died, she remembers deciding she wanted to be happy.

questions.q: What did Helen start to wonder while living abroad?
options: If her sadness was linked to her English childhood
Whether Danish people are really as happy as they seem
Whether she should write another book about Denmark
Whether she should move back home to England
questions.why: She wondered if her feelings were connected to being born in England, where showing emotions was discouraged.

questions.q: Which example of cultural difference is given?
options: In Spain, crying is seen as weak
In Japan, people sing and dance to show emotion
In England, people often cry in public
In Japan, crying is seen as weak and shameful
questions.why: Sam says in Japan crying is considered weak and shameful, while flamenco in Spain shows emotion.

questions.q: According to Professor Thomas Dixon, what did the word 'sad' first mean?
options: Lonely
Full
Tired
Empty
questions.why: He says the word 'sad' literally means sated or full.

questions.q: How is grief sometimes expressed in India?
options: Through poems and songs
By keeping completely silent
By people paid to cry for the family
By dancing in the street
questions.why: Neil says grief can be expressed by professional mourners paid to cry by the family.

questions.q: What does Professor Dixon say about the English reputation for hiding emotions?
options: It began mainly in Victorian and later times
It has always existed, since the Middle Ages
It started just after the Second World War
It is not true at all, and never has been
questions.why: He says it's by and large a Victorian, Edwardian and 20th-century characterisation.

questions.q: What do the presenters say really helps with sadness?
options: Drinking a little alcohol to relax
Keeping a stiff upper lip in public
Moving to a happier city or country
Talking to someone about your feelings
questions.why: Neil says it's talking to someone about your feelings that can really help.
